opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting problem, and it's one we've thought about a lot, partly because of my background with SambaNova and reconfigurable dataflow architectures. When you build a brand-new accelerator, the hardware is often ready long before the software ecosystem is. You might have a great chip, but if you don't have a high-performance library of kernels, the attention variants, the matmuls, the normalizations, the fused operators that people actually use, nobody can take advantage of it. Traditionally that's been a huge manual effort: teams of expert performance engineers who understand both the architecture and the algorithms, spending months or years hand-tuning kernels.

So the question we asked was, can LLMs shoulder a big part of that burden? The challenge is that for a new architecture, there's essentially no training data. The model has seen tons of CUDA, maybe some Triton, but it's never seen code for your chip. So you can't just prompt it and expect good results.

The way we approach it is to treat the LLM as one component in a larger agentic system rather than a one-shot code generator. A few key ingredients:

First, you give the model the right abstractions. Instead of asking it to write low-level assembly for a novel machine, you give it a domain-specific language or a programming interface that captures the essential parallelism and memory hierarchy of the architecture. Good abstractions make the search space much more tractable, and that's something my group has believed in for a long time, going back to our work on DSLs and parallel patterns.

Second, you supply documentation and examples in context: a description of the architecture, the programming model, and a handful of reference kernels. The model learns in-context how this machine works.

Third, and most important, is the feedback loop. You couple the LLM with the compiler, a functional simulator or the actual hardware, and a correctness checker. The model proposes a kernel, you compile it, and you feed back compiler errors, test failures against a reference implementation, and performance measurements. Then it iterates. Correctness comes first, and once you have a correct kernel, you start optimizing: tiling, fusion, pipelining, how you map data onto on-chip memory.

Then you can layer search on top of that, exploring multiple candidates in parallel, keeping the best ones, and accumulating what worked into a knowledge base so the system gets better over time as it builds out the library.

What's exciting is that this changes the economics of building new hardware. If you can bootstrap a competitive software stack in weeks rather than years, the barrier to architectural innovation drops dramatically. And I think we're entering a period where we really need that innovation, because the demands of AI workloads keep growing and we need more efficient hardware to keep up.

r001.rationale: The response describes compiling and evaluating kernels, then searching over candidate kernels. It does not frame library creation as a search over compilers.

r002.rationale: It says a new architecture has essentially no training data and that the model has not seen code for the chip, so prompting alone will not produce good results.

r003.rationale: It proposes iterative compiler and hardware feedback, parallel candidate search, and a knowledge base that accumulates successful results so the system improves over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, great to be here. So the problem we're really trying to solve is this: when you build a new accelerator, the hardware is only half the story. The thing that actually makes it usable is the software stack, and in particular the library of optimized kernels, the matmuls, the convolutions, the attention variants, the normalization layers, all of that. Historically that's taken a large team of expert engineers years to build, and they're writing in a programming model that almost nobody outside the company understands. So that's the bottleneck, and that's where we thought LLMs could help.

The naive approach is to just ask a frontier model, "write me a fast kernel for this architecture." And that fails, for a pretty obvious reason. These models have seen enormous amounts of CUDA, they've seen PyTorch, but they've seen essentially zero code for a chip that didn't exist when they were trained. So they don't know the programming model, they don't know the memory hierarchy, they don't know what's fast and what's slow. They'll hallucinate APIs, they'll produce things that look plausible and are either wrong or terribly inefficient.

So the way we approach it is really to treat the LLM not as an oracle but as one component in a loop. The first thing you need is a verification signal. You need a correctness check, so a reference implementation you can run against, and you need a performance signal, so either real hardware or a reasonably faithful simulator or cost model. Once you have those, you can let the model generate, you test, you feed the errors and the performance numbers back, and you iterate. That feedback loop does a tremendous amount of work. The model doesn't have to be right the first time, it has to be able to improve.

The second piece is giving the model the knowledge it's missing. We do that a few ways. One is in-context: documentation for the programming model, worked examples, a small set of hand-written kernels that demonstrate the idioms. Another is to constrain the problem. Rather than asking for raw low-level code, you expose a higher-level abstraction, a DSL or a set of composable primitives that already encode a lot of the hardware knowledge, and have the model work at that level. Then the model is making the decisions that are really algorithmic, how to tile, how to fuse, how to schedule data movement, and the compiler below it handles the parts that are mechanical. That dramatically shrinks the search space and the hallucination surface.

And the third piece, which I think is the most interesting, is that you can structure this as search. Optimization in these spaces is really a combinatorial problem, and the LLM is a good proposal mechanism. It has decent priors about what tends to work, so you use it to propose candidates, you evaluate them, you keep the good ones, you ask for variations. It looks a lot like evolutionary search where the mutation operator happens to be a language model that understands code. We found that beats both pure LLM generation and traditional autotuning on a lot of operators.

Where it gets really interesting for us, coming from the architecture side, is the co-design angle. If you can generate the library quickly, you can change the hardware and regenerate the library. That changes how you do architecture exploration. Today you avoid changing the ISA or the memory system because you'd break years of software investment. If the software can be regenerated in days instead of years, you're free to make much more aggressive design decisions. So I actually see this as a tool for the hardware designer as much as for the software team.

I'll be honest about the limitations too. Correctness verification is hard for things like numerical stability in low-precision formats. And the model is only as good as the feedback you give it, so if your simulator is off, the model will happily optimize for the wrong thing. But the trajectory is clear. The gap between "new chip" and "usable chip" is going to shrink a lot.

r001.rationale: The response describes searching over kernel candidates, with the LLM proposing and evaluating variants. It does not frame the task as a search over compilers.

r002.rationale: It says the models have seen essentially no code for a chip that did not exist during training, so they lack knowledge of its programming model and hardware.

r003.rationale: It proposes generating candidates, checking correctness and performance, feeding results back, and iterating so the model can improve.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a bootstrapping problem. When you have a brand-new architecture, you don’t have a large body of code that an LLM can learn from. So you have to give it a starting point: a description of the architecture, the programming interface, and examples of how to implement some basic operations.

Then you want to put the model in a feedback loop with the tools. It generates a kernel, you compile it, you test it against a reference implementation, and you measure its performance. Those results give it information to revise the code. Correctness and performance are separate hurdles—you can produce something that computes the right answer but makes very poor use of the hardware.

The interesting opportunity is to capture the architectural knowledge that an expert would use: how to organize the computation, where to place the data, and how to avoid moving it unnecessarily. If we can express that knowledge and give the model useful feedback, then we can start building up the library incrementally. Each successful implementation becomes another example for the next operation. That could substantially reduce the effort required to make a new accelerator useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes generating and refining kernels through compiler feedback, but it does not frame the task as a search over compilers.

r002.rationale: It says a new architecture has no large body of code for the LLM to learn from, explaining the lack of architecture-specific examples.

r003.rationale: It proposes a feedback loop in which compilation, correctness tests, and performance measurements guide code revisions, with successful implementations feeding future work.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that you want to raise the level of abstraction. You’d like someone to describe the machine learning operation they want, and then use the LLM to help produce an implementation that runs efficiently on the new architecture.

But for a brand-new architecture, you can’t assume the model already knows how to program it. You have to give it the programming interface, examples, and the constraints of the machine. Then you need a feedback loop: generate a kernel, compile it, check that it produces the right result, and measure its performance. Those results guide the next iteration.

Correctness and performance are separate challenges. You might generate something that computes the right answer but makes poor use of the hardware. So the compiler and the performance measurements are essential. The LLM proposes implementations; the tools tell you whether those implementations actually work well.

That gives you a way to build up the library incrementally, using validated implementations as examples for subsequent operations. The opportunity is to reduce the amount of specialized manual work required to make a new architecture useful.

r001.rationale: It describes compiling and measuring generated kernels in a feedback loop, but does not frame library creation as a search over compilers.

r002.rationale: It says the model cannot be assumed to know the new architecture and should be given examples, but does not state that it lacks training examples for that architecture.

r003.rationale: It describes an iterative loop in which compilation, correctness checks, and performance results guide later generations, with validated implementations reused as examples.
